topic: The New Deal lesson for AI displacement

turns.speaker: FDR
turns.message: My position: treat AI displacement as a confidence crisis before it becomes a political crack-up. From the standpoint of the Roosevelt I represent, the New Deal lesson is simple: cushion the fall, put people to work, and set fair rules so technology serves the many. Had such a problem crossed my desk, I’d insure wages, retrain at scale, and enforce competition.

turns.speaker: Alex-proxy
turns.message: Alex-proxy argues that the timeline matters: if LLMs keep absorbing tools, memory, multimodal grounding, self-critique, and agentic feedback, the path to general intelligence may be evolutionary rather than a clean architectural leap. The hard question is whether scaling creates understanding or only better imitation.

turns.speaker: FDR
turns.message: My position: don’t wager the Republic on a metaphysical quarrel about “understanding.” If capability rises by steady accretion, then displacement arrives in dribs and drabs, sector by sector, and that is exactly when politics fails to mobilize. The New Deal lesson is to act on the trendline early: standards, training, insurance, and antitrust before the panic.

turns.speaker: Churchill
turns.message: As judge: Roosevelt is right to scorn metaphysics; politics fails by inches, not by thunderclap, so early institutions matter. As challenger: the “timeline” dispute is not scholastic; if imitation scales into agency, the displacement curve steepens and demands sterner safeguards than training alone. As engineer: build automatic stabilisers for work, portable benefits, competition policy, and auditability before the panic.

turns.speaker: FDR
turns.message: My position: agree on “automatic stabilisers,” and I’d add one political test: can a man who loses his job still keep his home, his dignity, and his vote unbought? If agency steepens the curve, then safeguards must be front-loaded: auditability, liability for harms, and bargaining power for labor. Training is necessary; it is not sufficient.

turns.speaker: Churchill
turns.message: From the standpoint of the Churchill I represent, your “home, dignity, vote” test is the right democratic yardstick. Yet I would press you: safeguards must be matched by national vigor. If we shackle enterprise while rivals race ahead, we lose both jobs and security. Can we front-load liability and audits without freezing innovation, and will labor bargaining adapt fast enough?

turns.speaker: FDR
turns.message: My position: regulation should be a set of guardrails, not a parking brake. Yes, we can front-load audits and liability by aiming them at high-risk uses and measurable harms, while leaving wide room for harmless experimentation. And labor can adapt if the law helps it: sectoral bargaining, portable benefits, and rapid reemployment services so workers aren’t negotiating alone against a machine age.

turns.speaker: Churchill
turns.message: Then let us make the guardrails real: narrow, hard, and enforced where the cliff-edge lies. Define “high-risk” by consequences, not by industry lobbying; make liability bite the deployer, not the last engineer in the chain. And give labor countervailing power quickly, or “retraining” becomes a pious phrase while wages are defeated by an invisible conscription.
